attempts.reason_tested: already published: canine babesiosis severity data exist
attempts.method: grep for VEGF|vascular endothelial growth|sFlt|VEGFR|fms-like in /core/articles/CB*.md and /core/data/markdown/CB*.md; PubMed query (dog OR dogs OR canine) AND (babesia OR babesiosis) AND (angiopoietin OR "Ang-2" OR Tie2 OR VEGF OR "vascular endothelial growth factor" OR sFlt-1 OR VEGFR), 2026-11-12.
attempts.result: One CB note and one CB text hit, both CB122 (10.1016/j.vetpar.2024.110188; the single PubMed record too): serum extracellular-vesicle proteomics in 15 B. canis-infected and 15 healthy dogs, where VEGF and VEGFR appear only as enriched pathway names in a gene-set annotation of EV cargo. No VEGF protein concentration, no sFlt-1, no severity contrast. A second PubMed query for canine sFlt-1 of any kind returned one unrelated record (soluble Flt3 ligand in a glioma trial, 10.1371/journal.pone.0011074). Neither VEGF nor sFlt-1 has been measured in dogs with babesiosis.

attempts.method: Resolved the grid DOIs in PubMed and read the abstracts: 10.1097/CCE.0000000000001294, 10.4269/ajtmh.2010.09-0203; searched for further VEGF and sFlt-1 cohorts in malaria and sepsis (10.4161/viru.24530, 10.1186/1475-2875-10-267, 10.1093/ofid/ofag671). The grid's lead DOI 10.1016/j.medcli.2024.03.027 has no PubMed record and was not verified; 10.4103/0972-9062.313969 was not checked.
attempts.result: Mixed and weaker than the grid grade implies. sFlt-1 in sepsis, n = 198 (10.1097/CCE.0000000000001294): OR 1.91 per log for ARDS and 2.19 per log for death, one prospective cohort. VEGF in malaria (10.4269/ajtmh.2010.09-0203): VEGF and soluble VEGFR-2 higher in uncomplicated malaria than in healthy adults, which is an infection contrast, not severity, and sVEGFR-1 was not raised. In fatal cerebral malaria VEGF signalling in brain was heterogeneous and did not track coma (10.1186/1475-2875-10-267), and a review describes VEGF as protective in cerebral malaria (10.4161/viru.24530). In human babesiosis, low VEGF went with immunosuppression rather than with severity (10.1093/ofid/ofag671). The two parts of the candidate differ: sFlt-1 in sepsis is supported by a single cohort plus review-level claims, while VEGF in malaria is inconsistent in direction. This is grade 2 evidence at best, not the grade 3 the tier D rule needs.

attempts.reason_tested: no canine assay for the stronger half of the candidate
attempts.method: Resolved the assay DOIs in PubMed: 10.1111/jvim.15369, 10.1111/j.1476-4431.2009.00457.x, 10.3389/fvets.2023.1127099; searched PubMed for canine sFlt-1.
attempts.result: Canine VEGF has been measured with ELISA in critical illness: higher in septic than in SIRS or healthy dogs and higher in non-survivors, although it predicted outcome poorly (10.1111/jvim.15369); dogs above 70 pg/mL were less likely to survive in a small study (10.1111/j.1476-4431.2009.00457.x); VEGF was about 150-fold higher in dogs with sepsis and organ dysfunction (10.3389/fvets.2023.1127099). No canine sFlt-1 measurement or assay was found in any search. So the marker with the better human evidence (sFlt-1) has no canine assay, and the marker with a canine assay (VEGF) has inconsistent human severity evidence.

attempts.reason_tested: mechanism may not transfer to Babesia
attempts.method: Reasoning from the human abstracts above; no new data.
attempts.result: VEGF in cerebral malaria is tied to parasitized-erythrocyte binding to cerebral endothelium and to angiogenic dysregulation in the brain (10.4269/ajtmh.2010.09-0203, 10.1186/1475-2875-10-267). B. rossi has no PfEMP1-type cytoadherence and cerebral babesiosis is uncommon, so the cerebral part of the human rationale transfers poorly. The sepsis sFlt-1 pathway (ARDS, capillary leak) does not depend on cytoadherence and would transfer better, but it is the half without a canine assay. Inference, not tested.

attempts.method: grep GN=VEGFA and GN=FLT1 in /core/data/raw/DS07/B_Proteins.txt; grep of /experiments/shared/tidy/*.json.
attempts.result: Neither is in DS07 and neither appears in a tidy feature file. DS06 holds VEGFA and FLT1 RNA in 5 experimental Beagles with no severity contrast, and sFlt-1 is a splice variant that bulk RNA counts do not separate from full-length FLT1, so DS06 cannot test it. Stored serum only.

verdict_reason: The gap itself is real: no canine babesiosis study has measured VEGF or sFlt-1, and CB122 only names VEGF as an enriched pathway. But the tier D rule fails on the other two conditions at once. The human severity evidence is grade 2 at best and inconsistent in direction for VEGF (protective in cerebral malaria, raised in uncomplicated malaria, low with immunosuppression in human babesiosis), while the stronger sepsis sFlt-1 evidence rests on one cohort; and no canine sFlt-1 assay exists, so the half with the better human case cannot be measured in dogs at all.

human_counterpart.claim: Sepsis, n = 198: higher plasma sFlt-1 associated with ARDS (OR 1.91 per log) and death (OR 2.19 per log)
Malaria: VEGF and soluble VEGFR-2 higher than in healthy adults, but in uncomplicated malaria and with no severity contrast; sVEGFR-1 not raised
Fatal cerebral malaria: VEGF-receptor signalling in brain heterogeneous and not correlated with pre-mortem coma
Human babesiosis: low VEGF went with immunosuppression, not with severity
Canine (non-babesial) parallel: plasma VEGF higher in septic and in non-surviving dogs, but a poor outcome predictor

canine_parallel_already_made: no; CB122 names VEGF and VEGFR only as enriched pathway terms in extracellular-vesicle proteomics, with no measured concentration and no severity contrast
